title: Present Simple vs Present Continuous
summary: How to choose between habit and fact on one side and temporary, in-progress or changing situations on the other.

sections.heading: Permanent situations and temporary ones
sections.body:
The present simple describes what is generally or permanently true: habits, routines, scientific facts and long-term states. The present continuous describes what is in progress around the moment of speaking, or what holds only for a limited period.

The contrast is less about the clock than about how the speaker frames the situation. `He teaches at a technical college` presents the job as settled; `He is teaching at a technical college` suggests a temporary arrangement, perhaps a single term.

examples.right: Water freezes at zero degrees Celsius.
examples.wrong: Water is freezing at zero degrees Celsius.
examples.note: A permanent physical fact takes the present simple.

examples.right: I am staying with my cousin until the semester begins.
examples.wrong: I stay with my cousin until the semester begins.
examples.note: A temporary arrangement with a clear end point takes the continuous.

examples.right: The department publishes a review every quarter.
examples.note: A fixed routine, so the simple form.

sections.heading: Stative verbs stay simple
sections.body:
Some verbs name states rather than activities: **stative verbs** such as `know`, `believe`, `understand`, `own`, `belong`, `contain`, `seem`, `need`, `prefer` and `cost`. They normally appear in the simple form even when the state is true at this exact moment.

Arabic does not divide the present in this way, so there is a pull towards marking anything happening now with `am/is/are + -ing`. With a stative verb that reads as an error rather than as emphasis.

examples.note: `Know` is a state, not an activity in progress.

examples.wrong: The report is containing three appendices.
examples.note: `Contain` describes a fixed property of the document.

examples.right: She seems confident about the interview.
examples.wrong: She is seeming confident about the interview.
examples.note: `Seem` reports an impression, not something being done.

sections.heading: Verbs that shift meaning in the continuous
sections.body:
Several verbs are stative in one sense and dynamic in another. `Think` means 'hold an opinion' in the simple form and 'consider' in the continuous. `Have` means 'possess' in the simple form, but the activity expressions built on it (`have lunch`, `have a shower`, `have trouble`, `have a meeting`) take the continuous freely.

The same split governs `see` (perceive, or meet and visit), `taste` and `smell` (have a quality, or sample deliberately), and `look` (appear, or direct the eyes).

examples.right: I think the policy is misguided.
examples.wrong: I am thinking the policy is misguided.
examples.note: An opinion, so the simple form.

examples.right: She is thinking about applying for the scholarship.
examples.note: Here `think` means 'consider', which is an activity.

examples.right: He has a flat in the old quarter.
examples.wrong: He is having a flat in the old quarter.

examples.right: They are having a meeting on the third floor.
examples.note: `Have a meeting` is an activity, so the continuous is normal.

sections.heading: Trends, change and repeated irritation
sections.body:
The present continuous is the natural form for a situation that is developing: getting worse, rising, falling, becoming more common. Verbs of change take it constantly in essays and in graph descriptions.

With `always`, `constantly` or `forever`, the continuous adds exasperation or surprise at how often something happens. `He always arrives late` is a neutral statement of habit; `He is always arriving late` is a complaint.

examples.right: The cost of housing is rising faster than wages.
examples.note: A trend in progress rather than a timeless fact.

examples.right: Fewer students are choosing to study abroad.
examples.note: The continuous marks a change in behaviour over recent years.

examples.right: My neighbour is always parking across my driveway.
examples.note: `Always` with the continuous expresses irritation at the repetition.

examples.right: The train always leaves from platform four.
examples.wrong: The train is always leaving from platform four.
examples.note: A neutral timetable fact needs the simple form.

sections.heading: The present simple in academic English
sections.body:
Academic writing uses the present simple far more than the continuous. Research is reported in it (`Smith argues`, `the data suggest`, `the study finds`), general processes are described in it, and the standing truths of a field are stated in it.

The present simple also expresses scheduled future events fixed by a timetable or programme: departures, lectures, examinations, deadlines. Personal arrangements take the present continuous instead.

examples.right: Nguyen (2018) argues that the effect is overstated.
examples.wrong: Nguyen (2018) is arguing that the effect is overstated.
examples.note: Reporting verbs for published work take the present simple.

examples.right: The sample is heated to 80 degrees and then cooled slowly.
examples.note: Process descriptions stay in the simple form.

examples.right: The examination begins at nine on Tuesday.
examples.note: A timetabled event, so the present simple.

examples.right: I am meeting my tutor on Tuesday.
examples.note: A personal arrangement, so the present continuous.

slips: `I am knowing`, `I am understanding`, `I am believing`: state verbs keep the simple form even when the state holds right now.
`I am agree` and `I am think` blend the two present forms; the verbs are already finite, so write `I agree` and `I think`.
Reporting a source in the continuous (`The author is claiming that...`): use the present simple for what a text says.
`She is having a car`: `have` meaning possession is never continuous, although `have lunch` and `have a break` are.
Dropping the third-person `-s` (`The graph show a decline`): the continuous hides agreement inside `is/are`, so the `-s` is easy to forget when switching back.
Using `is always doing` for a neutral routine; keep that pattern for complaints and use the simple form for habits and timetables.

questions.prompt: At sea level, water ___ at 100 degrees Celsius.
questions.explain: A physical constant is a permanent fact and takes the present simple. `Is boiling` would describe one pan on one stove at this moment.

questions.prompt: At the moment the committee ___ the proposal, so no decision has been announced.
questions.explain: `At the moment` frames the review as unfinished and in progress, which is what the continuous marks.

questions.prompt: The 2019 study ___ that noise affects concentration in open-plan offices.
questions.explain: The findings of published research are reported in the present simple. `Is showing` would suggest something unfolding on a screen as we watch.

questions.prompt: She ___ about changing supervisors, but she has not made up her mind.
questions.explain: `Think` meaning 'consider' is an activity and takes the continuous, unlike `think` meaning 'believe', which stays simple.

questions.prompt: At present, Arctic sea ice ___ faster than the models of the 1990s predicted.
questions.explain: `At present` plus a developing trend calls for the continuous. The simple form would state the melting as a timeless property of ice.

questions.prompt: Once the sample ___ room temperature, it is weighed a second time.
questions.explain: Steps in a described procedure are given in the present simple, whatever the actual timing of the experiment.

questions.prompt: My flatmate ___ leaving unwashed pans in the sink, and it drives me mad.
questions.explain: `Is always + -ing` conveys irritation at a habit that keeps repeating. A bare `always` leaves `leaving` without a finite verb to hang on.

questions.prompt: I cannot talk now — I ___ lunch with a client.
questions.explain: `Have lunch` is an activity rather than possession, so it takes the continuous in a way that `have a car` never would.

questions.prompt: The archive ___ to the city council, although a charity runs it day to day.
questions.explain: `Belong` states a standing relationship and has no continuous use at all, however temporary the arrangement around it may be.

questions.prompt: The chef ___ the sauce to check the seasoning.
questions.explain: Here `taste` is something deliberately done; `the sauce tastes salty` describes a quality and would stay simple.

questions.prompt: The lecture ___ at nine and the seminar follows at eleven.
questions.explain: A timetabled future event takes the present simple. The continuous is reserved for personal arrangements such as `I am meeting my tutor`.

questions.prompt: Normally she ___ on the second floor, but this week she is working in the annexe.
questions.explain: `Normally` marks the settled arrangement, so the simple form; the second clause shows the continuous carrying the temporary exception.
